To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Flow past a circular cylinder is the canonical bluff-body problem. In the subcritical regime

convenient way to measure such configurations, but their results also depend on tank blockage.
These effects matter most at the moderate sizes and speeds typical of teaching and
mid-scale research facilities.

## 4. Discussion

### 4.1 Comparison with two-dimensional data

The measured C_D ≈ 1.15 lies at the upper end of the 1.0–1.2 range commonly reported for
two-dimensional cylinders in the subcritical regime **[CHECK: cite specific values, e.g.
Wieselsberger 1922; Roshko 1961; Zdravkovich 1997]**. At first sight this is surprising.
A cylinder with a free end and L/D = 12–24 would be expected to have a *lower* sectional drag
than a two-dimensional cylinder, because downwash from the tip raises the base pressure. For
example, classical data put C_D at roughly 0.8–0.9 for L/D ≈ 10–20 with one free end
**[CHECK: Wieselsberger; Zdravkovich 2003 vol. 2; Sumner 2013 review]**. Three effects
that raise the apparent C_D can offset this: tunnel blockage, free-surface wave drag, and
any force on the mounting/strut above the waterline. They are discussed below. As we
have no independent measurement of any one of them, we present the uncorrected values as the
primary result and the corrections as sensitivity estimates.

### 4.2 Blockage

The solid blockage ratio β = DL/(WH) is 2.3, 3.4 and 4.5 % for the three cylinders.
A Maskell-type bluff-body correction, C_D,c = C_D/(1 + m C_D β) with m ≈ 0.96 **[CHECK
constant and applicability to a partially-spanning model; consider West & Apelt 1982 or
Allen & Vincenti 1944 instead]**, reduces C_D by 2.5, 3.6 and 4.8 % respectively. The
corrected pooled value is 1.11.

The uncorrected C_D shows no measurable increase with blockage (1.143 → 1.157 from smallest to
largest), and that difference is well within the scatter. This suggests either that the
correction overestimates the effect for a cylinder spanning only 80 % of the depth, or that
it is masked by the competing Froude-number effect (§4.3). **[CHECK: decide whether to
headline corrected or uncorrected C_D.]**

The cylinders pierce the free surface, and the diameter Froude number reaches 2.2. At these
speeds a bow wave and a depressed wake form at the surface (**[TODO: any visual

# regenerate every number, table and figure in paper/draft.md from data/
# run from the project root:  python paper/make_paper_results.py
import glob
import os

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

OUT = "paper"
L = 0.60           # submerged length, m
W, H = 0.90, 0.75  # tank width, depth, m
EXCLUDE = {17: "load-cell zero shifted by +4.2 N after run; force drifts within window"}
T0, T1 = 3.0, 8.0  # steady averaging window, s
TARE = 1.0         # tare window t < TARE, s


def sensitivity(cal_file):
    c = pd.read_csv(cal_file)
    force = c.mass_g / 1000 * 9.81
    p = np.polyfit(force, c.voltage_V, 1)
    resid = c.voltage_V - np.polyval(p, force)
    return p[0], np.abs(resid).max() / p[0]


def load(f):
    # old DAQ: '#' header + comma; new DAQ (Mar 2026): ';' separated, t;V
    if ";" in open(f).readline():
        d = pd.read_csv(f, sep=";")
        return d.t.values, d.V.values
    d = pd.read_csv(f, comment="#")
    return d.time_s.values, d.loadcell_V.values


def water(T):
    # dynamic viscosity (Vogel fit) and density (Tanaka et al. 2001 form), T in C
    mu = 2.414e-5 * 10 ** (247.8 / (T + 273.15 - 140))
    rho = 999.974950 * (1 - (T - 3.983035) ** 2 * (T + 301.797)
                        / (522528.9 * (T + 69.34881)))
    return mu / rho, rho


cal = {"2025-09": sensitivity("data/calibration/loadcell_2025-09.csv"),
       "2026-03": sensitivity("data/calibration/loadcell_2026-03.csv")}
log = pd.read_csv("data/run_log.csv")

rows, traces = [], {}
for f in sorted(glob.glob("data/raw/*/run_*.csv")):
    run = int(os.path.basename(f)[4:7])
    sens = cal["2026-03" if "/2026-" in f else "2025-09"][0]
    t, v = load(f)
    F = (v - v[t < TARE].mean()) / sens
    st = (t > T0) & (t < T1)
    x = F[st] - F[st].mean()
    fs = 1 / np.median(np.diff(t))
    P = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x * np.hanning(len(x)))) ** 2
    freq = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1 / fs)
    blocks = [b.mean() for b in np.array_split(F[st], 10)]
    rows.append(dict(run=run, F=F[st].mean(), F_rms=F[st].std(),
                     F_se=np.std(blocks, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(blocks)),
                     F_end=F[t > t.max() - 1].mean(),
                     f_drag=freq[1:][np.argmax(P[1:])], df=freq[1]))
    traces[run] = (t, F)

r = pd.DataFrame(rows).merge(log, left_on="run", right_on="run_id")
D = r.diameter_mm / 1000
U = r.speed_m_s
r["nu"], r["rho"] = water(r.water_temp_c)
r["Re"] = U * D / r.nu
r["Re_20C"] = U * D / 1.004e-6
r["Cd"] = r.F / (0.5 * r.rho * U ** 2 * D * L)
r["Cd_se"] = r.F_se / (0.5 * r.rho * U ** 2 * D * L)
r["St"] = 0.5 * r.f_drag * D / U  # drag fluctuates at twice the shedding frequency
r["Fr"] = U / np.sqrt(9.81 * D)
r["AR"] = L / D
r["blockage"] = D * L / (W * H)
r["Cd_maskell"] = r.Cd / (1 + 0.96 * r.Cd * r.blockage)  # sensitivity only
r["excluded"] = r.run.isin(EXCLUDE)
r.to_csv(f"{OUT}/results_all_runs.csv", index=False)

g = r[~r.excluded]
order = ["1in", "1.5in", "2in"]
summ = (g.groupby("cylinder")
        .agg(D_mm=("diameter_mm", "first"), AR=("AR", "first"),
             blockage_pct=("blockage", lambda b: 100 * b.iloc[0]),
             n=("Cd", "size"), Re_min=("Re", "min"), Re_max=("Re", "max"),
             Fr_min=("Fr", "min"), Fr_max=("Fr", "max"),
             Cd_mean=("Cd", "mean"), Cd_sd=("Cd", "std"),
             Cd_maskell=("Cd_maskell", "mean"), St_mean=("St", "mean"), St_sd=("St", "std"))
        .loc[order])

with open(f"{OUT}/numbers.txt", "w") as fh:
    p = lambda *a: print(*a, file=fh)
    for k, (s, e) in cal.items():

    p(f"water T {r.water_temp_c.min()}-{r.water_temp_c.max()} C, "

    p(f"Re (20C nu) / Re (actual nu): {(r.Re_20C / r.Re).min():.3f}-{(r.Re_20C / r.Re).max():.3f}")

    p(f"run 17: zero after run {r.set_index('run').F_end[17]:.2f} N, Cd {r.set_index('run').Cd[17]:.3f}")
    p(f"pooled slope dCd/dlog10(Re) {np.polyfit(np.log10(g.Re), g.Cd, 1)[0]:.3f}")
    p(f"pooled slope dCd/dFr {np.polyfit(g.Fr, g.Cd, 1)[0]:.3f}")
    p("")
    p(summ.round(4).to_string())

plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 9, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,

                     "axes.labelcolor": "#0b0b0b", "legend.frameon": False})
COL = {"1in": "#2a78d6", "1.5in": "#eb6834", "2in": "#1baf7a"}
MK = {"1in": "o", "1.5in": "s", "2in": "^"}
LAB = {c: f"D = {r[r.cylinder == c].diameter_mm.iloc[0]:.1f} mm" for c in order}
GRID = dict(color="#e4e3df", lw=0.6)

# Fig 1: example trace
t, F = traces[5]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.6))
ax.axvspan(T0, T1, color="#e4e3df", lw=0)
ax.plot(t, F, color="#2a78d6", lw=0.6)

ax.set_xlabel("t (s)")

fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(f"{OUT}/fig1_timeseries_run005.png", dpi=300)

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

mid-scale research facilities.

Streamwise force was measured with a single-axis load cell **[TODO: make/model, capacity, how

sampled at 200 Hz **[TODO: DAQ hardware, anti-alias filtering]**. Each run recorded 12 s of

Force was F(t) = [V(t) − V₀]/S, where S is the calibration sensitivity. The mean drag F̄ is
the average of F(t) over 3 s < t < 8 s (Fig. 1). In every retained run the force reaches its
plateau (within 5 % of the mean) by t ≈ 2.5 s and stays there until t ≈ 9.0 s, so the window

  C_D = F̄ / (½ ρ U² D L),

and the Reynolds and diameter Froude numbers are

  Re = U D / ν,  Fr_D = U / √(g D).

# run from the project root:  python paper/make_paper_results.py
import glob
import os

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

OUT = "paper"
L = 0.60           # submerged length, m
W, H = 0.90, 0.75  # tank width, depth, m
EXCLUDE = {17: "load-cell zero shifted by +4.2 N after run; force drifts within window"}
T0, T1 = 3.0, 8.0  # steady averaging window, s
TARE = 1.0         # tare window t < TARE, s


def sensitivity(cal_file):
    c = pd.read_csv(cal_file)
    force = c.mass_g / 1000 * 9.81
    p = np.polyfit(force, c.voltage_V, 1)
    resid = c.voltage_V - np.polyval(p, force)
    return p[0], np.abs(resid).max() / p[0]


def load(f):
    # old DAQ: '#' header + comma; new DAQ (Mar 2026): ';' separated, t;V
    if ";" in open(f).readline():
        d = pd.read_csv(f, sep=";")
        return d.t.values, d.V.values
    d = pd.read_csv(f, comment="#")
    return d.time_s.values, d.loadcell_V.values


def water(T):
    # dynamic viscosity (Vogel fit) and density (Tanaka et al. 2001 form), T in C
    mu = 2.414e-5 * 10 ** (247.8 / (T + 273.15 - 140))
    rho = 999.974950 * (1 - (T - 3.983035) ** 2 * (T + 301.797)
                        / (522528.9 * (T + 69.34881)))
    return mu / rho, rho


cal = {"2025-09": sensitivity("data/calibration/loadcell_2025-09.csv"),
       "2026-03": sensitivity("data/calibration/loadcell_2026-03.csv")}
log = pd.read_csv("data/run_log.csv")

rows, traces = [], {}
for f in sorted(glob.glob("data/raw/*/run_*.csv")):
    run = int(os.path.basename(f)[4:7])
    sens = cal["2026-03" if "/2026-" in f else "2025-09"][0]
    t, v = load(f)
    F = (v - v[t < TARE].mean()) / sens
    st = (t > T0) & (t < T1)
    x = F[st] - F[st].mean()
    fs = 1 / np.median(np.diff(t))
    P = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x * np.hanning(len(x)))) ** 2
    freq = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1 / fs)
    blocks = [b.mean() for b in np.array_split(F[st], 10)]
    rows.append(dict(run=run, F=F[st].mean(), F_rms=F[st].std(),
                     F_se=np.std(blocks, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(blocks)),
                     F_end=F[t > t.max() - 1].mean(),
                     f_drag=freq[1:][np.argmax(P[1:])], df=freq[1]))
    traces[run] = (t, F)

D = r.diameter_mm / 1000
U = r.speed_m_s
r["nu"], r["rho"] = water(r.water_temp_c)
r["Re"] = U * D / r.nu
r["Re_20C"] = U * D / 1.004e-6
r["Cd"] = r.F / (0.5 * r.rho * U ** 2 * D * L)
r["Cd_se"] = r.F_se / (0.5 * r.rho * U ** 2 * D * L)
r["St"] = 0.5 * r.f_drag * D / U  # drag fluctuates at twice the shedding frequency
r["Fr"] = U / np.sqrt(9.81 * D)
r["AR"] = L / D
r["blockage"] = D * L / (W * H)
r["Cd_maskell"] = r.Cd / (1 + 0.96 * r.Cd * r.blockage)  # sensitivity only
r["excluded"] = r.run.isin(EXCLUDE)
r.to_csv(f"{OUT}/results_all_runs.csv", index=False)

g = r[~r.excluded]
order = ["1in", "1.5in", "2in"]
summ = (g.groupby("cylinder")
        .agg(D_mm=("diameter_mm", "first"), AR=("AR", "first"),
             blockage_pct=("blockage", lambda b: 100 * b.iloc[0]),
             n=("Cd", "size"), Re_min=("Re", "min"), Re_max=("Re", "max"),
             Fr_min=("Fr", "min"), Fr_max=("Fr", "max"),
             Cd_mean=("Cd", "mean"), Cd_sd=("Cd", "std"),
             Cd_maskell=("Cd_maskell", "mean"), St_mean=("St", "mean"), St_sd=("St", "std"))
        .loc[order])
summ["dCd_dlogRe"] = [np.polyfit(np.log10(g[g.cylinder == c].Re), g[g.cylinder == c].Cd, 1)[0]
                      for c in order]
summ.to_csv(f"{OUT}/summary_by_cylinder.csv")

with open(f"{OUT}/numbers.txt", "w") as fh:
    p = lambda *a: print(*a, file=fh)
    for k, (s, e) in cal.items():
        p(f"calibration {k}: sensitivity {s:.5f} V/N, max residual {e * 1000:.1f} mN")
    p(f"water T {r.water_temp_c.min()}-{r.water_temp_c.max()} C, "
      f"nu {r.nu.min():.3e}-{r.nu.max():.3e} m2/s")
    p(f"Re (20C nu) / Re (actual nu): {(r.Re_20C / r.Re).min():.3f}-{(r.Re_20C / r.Re).max():.3f}")
    p(f"Re range {g.Re.min():.0f}-{g.Re.max():.0f}; Fr range {g.Fr.min():.2f}-{g.Fr.max():.2f}")
    p(f"pooled Cd {g.Cd.mean():.3f} +/- {g.Cd.std():.3f} (sd, n={len(g)})")
    p(f"pooled Cd maskell-corrected {g.Cd_maskell.mean():.3f}")
    p(f"pooled St {g.St.mean():.3f} +/- {g.St.std():.3f}; FFT bin St resolution "
      f"{(0.5 * g.df * g.diameter_mm / 1000 / g.speed_m_s).min():.3f}-"
      f"{(0.5 * g.df * g.diameter_mm / 1000 / g.speed_m_s).max():.3f}")
    p(f"max within-run SE of mean / mean: {(g.F_se / g.F).max() * 100:.2f} %")
    p(f"max |zero after run| (kept runs): {g.F_end.abs().max() * 1000:.1f} mN")
    p(f"run 17: zero after run {r.set_index('run').F_end[17]:.2f} N, Cd {r.set_index('run').Cd[17]:.3f}")
    p(f"pooled slope dCd/dlog10(Re) {np.polyfit(np.log10(g.Re), g.Cd, 1)[0]:.3f}")
    p(f"pooled slope dCd/dFr {np.polyfit(g.Fr, g.Cd, 1)[0]:.3f}")
    p("")
    p(summ.round(4).to_string())

# ---- figures ----
plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 9, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
                     "axes.edgecolor": "#52514e", "xtick.color": "#52514e", "ytick.color": "#52514e",
                     "axes.labelcolor": "#0b0b0b", "legend.frameon": False})
COL = {"1in": "#2a78d6", "1.5in": "#eb6834", "2in": "#1baf7a"}
MK = {"1in": "o", "1.5in": "s", "2in": "^"}
LAB = {c: f"D = {r[r.cylinder == c].diameter_mm.iloc[0]:.1f} mm" for c in order}
GRID = dict(color="#e4e3df", lw=0.6)

# Fig 1: example trace
t, F = traces[5]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.6))
ax.axvspan(T0, T1, color="#e4e3df", lw=0)
ax.plot(t, F, color="#2a78d6", lw=0.6)
ax.text((T0 + T1) / 2, F.max() * 1.07, "averaging window", ha="center", color="#52514e")
ax.set_xlabel("t (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("F (N)")
ax.set_ylim(-0.2, F.max() * 1.18)
ax.grid(axis="y", **GRID)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(f"{OUT}/fig1_timeseries_run005.png", dpi=300)

# Fig 2: Cd vs Re
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.6))
for c in order:
    s = g[g.cylinder == c]
    ax.plot(s.Re, s.Cd, MK[c], ms=6, color=COL[c], mec="#fcfcfb", mew=0.8, label=LAB[c])
x = r[r.excluded]
ax.plot(x.Re, x.Cd, "^", ms=6, mfc="none", mec="#8a8984", mew=1, label="run 17 (excluded)")
ax.axhline(g.Cd.mean(), color="#8a8984", lw=0.8, ls="--", zorder=0)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xticks([5e3, 1e4, 2e4, 5e4], ["5000", "10 000", "20 000", "50 000"])
ax.set_xlabel("Re = UD/ν")
ax.set_ylabel("$C_D$")
ax.grid(**GRID)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", ncol=2)
ax.set_ylim(1.0, 1.42)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(f"{OUT}/fig2_cd_vs_re.png", dpi=300)

# Fig 3: St vs Re
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 2.8))
for c in order:
    s = g[g.cylinder == c]
    ax.plot(s.Re, s.St, MK[c], ms=6, color=COL[c], mec="#fcfcfb", mew=0.8, label=LAB[c])
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xticks([5e3, 1e4, 2e4, 5e4], ["5000", "10 000", "20 000", "50 000"])
ax.set_xlabel("Re = UD/ν")
ax.set_ylabel("St = $f_s D/U$")
ax.set_ylim(0.15, 0.25)
ax.grid(**GRID)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", ncol=3)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(f"{OUT}/fig3_st_vs_re.png", dpi=300)
print(open(f"{OUT}/numbers.txt").read())

has a cross-section of 0.90 m (width) × 0.75 m (water depth) and a length of **[TODO]** m.
The models were smooth circular cylinders of nominal diameter 1, 1.5 and 2 in (D = 25.4, 38.1
and 50.8 mm), made of **[TODO: material, surface finish, straightness]**. Each cylinder was
mounted vertically from the carriage and pierced the free surface, with a submerged length of
L = 0.60 m. This leaves a gap of about 0.15 m between the free (lower) end and the tank floor.
**[TODO: confirm gap; describe end condition — plain cut end? end plate?]** The geometric

**Table 1.** Model geometry and test conditions (run 17 excluded; see §3.3).

| D (mm) | L/D | Solid blockage DL/(WH) | Runs | Water T (°C) | Re range | Fr_D range |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 25.4 | 23.6 | 2.3 % | 10 | 16.9–17.6 | 4 690–26 250 | 0.40–2.20 |
| 38.1 | 15.7 | 3.4 % | 10 | 13.7–14.3 | 6 480–36 200 | 0.33–1.80 |
| 50.8 | 11.8 | 4.5 % | 9 | 15.0–15.6 | 8 940–49 910 | 0.28–1.56 |

### 2.2 Carriage and test matrix

Each cylinder was towed at ten nominal speeds, U = 0.2, 0.3, …, 1.1 m s⁻¹, in a single
session per cylinder: 25.4 mm on 14 Oct 2025, 50.8 mm on 3 Nov 2025 and 38.1 mm on 12 Mar
2026. Water temperature was recorded for every run (`data/run_log.csv`).
**[TODO: carriage drive, speed control and accuracy, acceleration distance, and the waiting
time between runs to let the tank settle. The run log notes a small residual wave from the
previous run for run 4. Each speed was run once; there were no repeat runs.]**

### 2.3 Force measurement and calibration

Streamwise force was measured with a single-axis load cell **[TODO: make/model, capacity, how
the cylinder is mounted to it, and whether it measures force or moment about a pivot]**,
sampled at 200 Hz **[TODO: DAQ hardware, anti-alias filtering]**. Each run recorded 12 s of
data, with the carriage starting at t ≈ 1.5 s.

Before each campaign the load cell was calibrated in situ with dead weights of 0–2000 g,
loaded and unloaded (Fig. — optional; data in `data/calibration/`). Linear fits gave
sensitivities of 0.02001 V N⁻¹ (Sept 2025, used for the 25.4 and 50.8 mm cylinders) and
0.02129 V N⁻¹ (March 2026, after the load cell was remounted, used for the 38.1 mm cylinder).
Maximum residuals were 16 and 17 mN respectively, and loading/unloading hysteresis was within
the same band. **[CHECK: describe how the calibration load was applied — along the drag axis at
the cylinder's centre of pressure?]**

### 2.4 Data reduction

For each run, the zero offset was the mean voltage over t < 1 s, while the carriage was at rest.
Force was F(t) = [V(t) − V₀]/S, where S is the calibration sensitivity. The mean drag F̄ is
the average of F(t) over 3 s < t < 8 s (Fig. 1). In every retained run the force reaches its
plateau (within 5 % of the mean) by t ≈ 2.5 s and stays there until t ≈ 9.0 s, so the window
is inside the steady-tow interval. Changing it to 3.5–7.5 s shifts F̄ by at most 0.2 %.

The drag coefficient is based on the submerged frontal area,

  C_D = F̄ / (½ ρ U² D L),

and the Reynolds and diameter Froude numbers are

  Re = U D / ν,  Fr_D = U / √(g D).

Here ρ(T) and ν(T) are evaluated at the water temperature recorded for each run. **[Note:
the earlier analysis notebook used ν at 20 °C. The water was 13.7–17.6 °C, so that
overestimated Re by 6–17 %; C_D is essentially unaffected (ρ changes by < 0.1 %).]**

The shedding frequency f_s comes from the peak of the Hann-windowed spectrum of the drag
fluctuation over the same 5 s window. The streamwise force oscillates at twice the shedding
frequency, so St = f_s D/U = ½ f_peak D/U. The 5 s record limits the frequency resolution to
0.2 Hz, so St is resolved to ±0.002 at the highest speeds and only to ±0.025 at the
lowest. **[CHECK: Fig. 1 suggests the dominant oscillation is at 2f_s, as expected for drag on a
cylinder. Confirm that the load cell's natural frequency is well above the highest f_peak
(17 Hz) so the fluctuations are not structural resonance.]**

![Fig. 1](fig1_timeseries_run005.png)

**Fig. 1.** Drag force time series for D = 25.4 mm, U = 0.6 m s⁻¹ (run 5, Re = 1.41 × 10⁴). The
shaded band marks the averaging window.

---

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Drag coefficient

Figure 2 and Table 2 give the drag coefficient for all runs. With run 17 excluded (§3.3),
C_D falls between 1.09 and 1.22 with no systematic dependence on diameter:

**Table 2.** Mean drag coefficient and Strouhal number per cylinder (mean ± s.d. over runs).

| D (mm) | n | C_D | C_D, Maskell-corrected* | St | dC_D / d log₁₀Re |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 25.4 | 10 | 1.143 ± 0.033 | 1.116 | 0.200 ± 0.002 | +0.11 |
| 38.1 | 10 | 1.152 ± 0.026 | 1.111 | 0.199 ± 0.004 | +0.07 |
| 50.8 | 9 | 1.157 ± 0.034 | 1.102 | 0.202 ± 0.003 | −0.01 |
| all | 29 | 1.151 ± 0.030 | 1.110 | 0.200 ± 0.003 | +0.06 |

\* Sensitivity estimate only; see §4.2.

The mean values for the three diameters differ by 0.014, well inside the run-to-run scatter.
Across the full range of 4.7 × 10³ ≤ Re ≤ 5.0 × 10⁴, a pooled fit gives
dC_D/d log₁₀Re = 0.06. That is a change of about 0.06 per decade, comparable to the scatter.
The smallest cylinder shows the steepest rise (+0.11 per decade), but its ten points also span
the widest Froude-number range (§4.3), so the trend cannot be attributed to Re alone.

![Fig. 2](fig2_cd_vs_re.png)

**Fig. 2.** Drag coefficient against Reynolds number. Dashed line: pooled mean C_D = 1.151.
Open symbol: run 17, excluded from all statistics (§3.3). The statistical uncertainty of each
run's mean (2 × standard error, from ten 0.5 s block means) is < 0.7 % of C_D, smaller than
the symbols.

### 3.2 Strouhal number

The shedding Strouhal number (Fig. 3) is St = 0.200 ± 0.003 across all diameters and speeds,
consistent with the accepted subcritical value of ≈ 0.2 (e.g. Norberg 2003). The agreement
supports the Reynolds-number scaling, independently of the force calibration.

![Fig. 3](fig3_st_vs_re.png)

**Fig. 3.** Shedding Strouhal number from the dominant drag-fluctuation frequency. The scatter
at low Re reflects the 0.2 Hz spectral resolution of the 5 s window.

### 3.3 Excluded run

Run 17 (D = 50.8 mm, U = 0.8 m s⁻¹) was flagged in the lab notes ("zero off after the run").
After the carriage stops, the load-cell signal settles 4.2 N away from its pre-run zero. In
every retained run it returns to within 4 mN. The run's force also rises steadily from
12.7 N to 13.7 N across the averaging window, whereas the retained runs change by < 0.5 %
between the two halves of the window. The resulting C_D = 1.355 is 0.2 above every other
point, so we attribute the run to load-cell zero drift and exclude it. **[TODO/CHECK:
